grammar_questions.question:
(1) The city plans to renovate the old train depot into a public market. (2) The renovated market will serve as a year-round venue for local vendors.

What is the best way to combine the sentences to clarify the relationship between the ideas?

options.A: The city plans to renovate the old train depot into a public market, but this market will serve as a year-round venue for local vendors.
options.B: Intending to serve as a year-round venue for local vendors, the old train depot will be renovated into a public market by the city.
options.C: The city plans to renovate the old train depot into a public market; afterward, this market will serve as a year-round venue for local vendors.
options.D: Although the city plans to renovate the old train depot into a public market, this market will serve as a year-round venue for local vendors.

solution.exhibit_text:
(C) is correct because the semicolon plus “afterward” accurately shows the sequence: the renovation happens first, and the market's new role as a vendor venue follows. (A) and (D) use “but”/“Although,” which wrongly suggest a contradiction between the two ideas, which actually agree. (B) misplaces the introductory phrase “Intending to serve as a year-round venue...” so it appears to modify “the old train depot” itself rather than the market role, and its passive “will be renovated...by the city” construction is also awkward.

**The concept:** When you combine sentences using a connecting word — because, although, while, which, and, but, since — that word has to accurately describe how the two ideas really relate: does one cause the other? Contradict it? Just add detail? Work out the real relationship in plain language first, then check that each answer choice's connecting word actually matches it. A word like "although" promises a contradiction; if the ideas don't actually conflict, "although" is wrong no matter how smooth the sentence sounds.

options.C: Intending to serve as a critical staging point for future missions to Mars, the Moon will be used to establish a base camp by NASA's Artemis program.
options.D: Although NASA's Artemis program plans to establish a base camp on the Moon, this lunar presence will serve as a critical staging point for future missions to Mars.

grammar_questions.question:
(1) Sourdough bread has become increasingly popular, but it requires significant patience and skill. (2) Many bakers maintain their starters for years, feeding them daily to keep the wild yeast active. (3) The recipe for a good sourdough loaf requires a strong starter, and patience, which is needed to develop the proper texture. (4) Professional bakeries, many of which only use wild yeast, sell extra starter to beginners who skip the lengthy cultivation process.

Which pair of revisions need to be made in this paragraph?

options.A: Sentence 1: Delete the comma after popular AND change requires to require.
options.B: Sentence 2: Delete the comma after years AND change feeding to feeds.
options.C: Sentence 3: Delete the comma after starter AND change is to are.
options.D: Sentence 4: Delete the comma after bakeries AND change sell to sells.

solution.exhibit_text:
Sentence 3 has two errors: the comma after “starter” wrongly separates “a strong starter” from “patience” as though “patience” were a third item or a second sentence, when “and” here just links two items — the comma should be deleted. And “is” should be “are” because the subject of “which” is the full compound “a strong starter and patience” (plural), not just “patience” alone.

**The concept:** A comma goes before "and" when it separates the last item in a list of three or more, or when "and" is joining two complete, independent sentences. But when "and" is just linking two verbs or phrases that share the same subject, no comma belongs before it — adding one wrongly suggests a third list item, or a second full sentence, that isn't actually there.

**The concept:** Subject-verb agreement means the verb has to match whether its subject is singular or plural ("the museum becomes," not "the museum become"). Pronoun agreement works the same way — a pronoun has to match the number of the noun it refers back to. These two rules often get tested together in the same sentence, so check both the verb and any pronouns against their subject/antecedent, not just one or the other.

grammar_questions.question:
(1) Maria and Elena have been taking piano lessons since they were seven years old. (2) Her aunt was a concert pianist and still gives both girls private coaching on weekends. (3) The sisters always practice duets together before their monthly recitals. (4) Both girls hope to audition for the youth symphony next year.

Which sentence in the paragraph contains an error in construction? There is only one error in construction.

solution.exhibit_text:
“Her aunt” in sentence 2 is vague because it's unclear whether “her” refers to Maria or to Elena — both are equally possible antecedents.

**The concept:** A pronoun needs exactly one clear noun it could be replacing. If a sentence has two or more people or things it could plausibly point to — or if it doesn't clearly point to anything — the pronoun is vague. Fix it by swapping the pronoun back out for the actual name or noun, or by rewriting the sentence so only one candidate is possible.

grammar_questions.question:
Deep within Echo Canyon, a single clap can produce several distinct echoes because the canyon's layered rock walls send the sound back to the listener.

Which revision to the words **send the sound back to the listener** uses the most precise language?

options.A: reflect the sound waves off nearby surfaces
options.B: bounce the sound waves around the general area
options.C: reflect the sound waves off each successive rock ledge in sequence
options.D: move the sound waves back toward where they came from

solution.exhibit_text:
“reflect the sound waves off each successive rock ledge in sequence” is the most precise option — it names the exact surfaces (the rock ledges) and explains the order (in sequence) that produces multiple distinct echoes. **The concept:** Precise language replaces vague, generic words ("things," "a big distance," "what was happening") with specific, concrete details — exact names, numbers, or nouns — that tell the reader precisely what's being described. When comparing answer choices, prefer the one with the most specific, checkable information instead of just restating the same vagueness in fancier words.

Christopher Latham Sholes is credited with inventing the first, commercial typewriter, a machine with separate metal arms for each letter, more mechanically complex than the electric typewriters of today which use a single rotating ball to strike every character.

Which revision corrects the sentence?

options.B: Delete the comma after **typewriter** AND delete the comma after **letter**.
options.C: Insert a comma after **character** AND delete the comma after **first**.
options.D: Delete the comma after **letter** AND insert a comma after **today**.

solution.exhibit_text:
The comma after “first” must be deleted — “first” and “commercial” are not coordinate adjectives (you wouldn't say “commercial first typewriter”), so no comma belongs between them. A comma is needed after “today” because “which use a single rotating ball...” is a nonessential clause giving extra detail about “today's electric typewriters,” not essential information.

**The concept:** When two adjectives both independently describe the same noun (you could say them in either order, or put "and" between them — "calm and patient," "patient and calm"), they need a comma between them. If the adjectives don't work that way — if one adjective is really describing the adjective+noun combo together (like "bright red car," where you wouldn't say "red bright car") — no comma is needed. Test it: can you swap the order or insert "and"? If yes, add the comma.

options.D: Sentence 4: Delete the comma after **rehearsal** AND change **will** to **would**.

solution.exhibit_text:
Deleting the comma after “cords” correctly joins “reliable extension cords” and “extra gel filters” as a single two-item subject, since “and” here just links two things — no comma belongs before it. “Is” must become “are” to agree with that full compound subject, “reliable extension cords and extra gel filters.”

**The concept:** A comma goes before "and" when it separates the last item in a list of three or more, or when "and" is joining two complete, independent sentences. But when "and" is just linking two verbs or phrases that share the same subject, no comma belongs before it — adding one wrongly suggests a third list item, or a second full sentence, that isn't actually there.

**The concept:** Subject-verb agreement means the verb has to match whether its subject is singular or plural ("the museum becomes," not "the museum become"). Pronoun agreement works the same way — a pronoun has to match the number of the noun it refers back to. These two rules often get tested together in the same sentence, so check both the verb and any pronouns against their subject/antecedent, not just one or the other.

grammar_questions.question:
(1) The young chef prepared a bold inventive dish for the competition's final round. (2) Judges were asked to score each plate on presentation, flavor, and originality. (3) Her sauce combined three unexpected ingredients that surprised even veteran tasters. (4) The winning dish later appeared on the restaurant's permanent menu.

Which sentence contains an error in its construction and should be revised?

solution.exhibit_text:
In sentence 1, “bold” and “inventive” are coordinate adjectives of equal weight describing “dish” — you could say “inventive, bold dish” or “bold and inventive dish” — so they need a comma between them: “a bold, inventive dish.”

**The concept:** When two adjectives both independently describe the same noun (you could say them in either order, or put "and" between them — "calm and patient," "patient and calm"), they need a comma between them. If the adjectives don't work that way — if one adjective is really describing the adjective+noun combo together (like "bright red car," where you wouldn't say "red bright car") — no comma is needed. Test it: can you swap the order or insert "and"? If yes, add the comma.

(2) Yalina's job is to open the box and pour the pancake mix into a bowl, slowly adding water, eggs, melted butter, and blueberries. (3) Michael uses a wooden spoon to vigorously stir the mixture until it is smooth, and Malcolm helps Granddad carefully pour the batter onto a griddle one-fourth cup at a time. base_question.question: Which pair of revisions is needed to correct the errors in the paragraph?

options.A: Sentence 1: Delete the comma after **Yalina**, AND change **their** to **her**.

options.D: Sentence 4: Change **they start** to **it starts**, AND insert a comma after **sweet**.

solution.exhibit_text: In sentence 4, the plural pronoun “they” wrongly refers to the singular antecedent “each pancake,” so it should be “it starts.” Separately, “sweet” and “delicious” are coordinate adjectives of equal weight describing “breakfast,” so they need a comma between them.

grammar_questions.question:
(1) The robotics team spent months building their competition robot. (2) Judges evaluate each robot on speed, accuracy, and design creativity. (3) The team's robot completed the obstacle course faster than any other entry. (4) When the robot crosses the finish line, they immediately stop moving and wait for the next command.

Which sentence contains an error in its construction and should be revised?

solution.exhibit_text:
In sentence 4, the plural pronoun “they” wrongly refers to the singular antecedent “the robot,” so it should be “it immediately stops moving.”

**The concept:** A pronoun has to match the number of the noun it's replacing — singular noun, singular pronoun ("it"); plural noun, plural pronoun ("they"/"them"). Find the antecedent (the noun the pronoun stands in for), check if it's one thing or more than one thing, and make sure the pronoun matches. A list of someone's traits or parts ("its mouth, skin, and coloring") can look plural, but it's still describing one single subject.

grammar_questions.question:
(1) Hoping to land a job in tech within six months, the coding bootcamp requires forty hours of class time each week. (2) Students work in small groups to complete weekly coding projects. (3) Instructors review each project individually before the next module begins. (4) Graduates receive a certificate and access to the bootcamp's job-placement network.

Which sentence contains an error in its construction and should be revised?

solution.exhibit_text:
Sentence 1 opens with “Hoping to land a job in tech within six months,” which should describe the students, but as written it attaches to “the coding bootcamp” instead — illogical, since a bootcamp program itself can't hope to land a job.

**The concept:** A describing phrase attaches to whatever noun sits closest to it, usually the noun right after it. If that's not the noun the phrase is actually meant to describe, the sentence ends up saying something illogical — a modifier "dangling" with nothing correct to attach to, or "misplaced" and describing the wrong thing. Find the noun the phrase is logically describing, then make sure that noun (not some other noun that happens to be nearby) is the one sitting right next to it.
